children: By Jack Gillum, Alison Sider, James Benedict and Cam Pollack
The Federal Aviation Administration's move to halt all flight departures Friday afternoon shows the fragility of America's air-traffic control infrastructure.

The extraordinary step, taken in response to disruptions in air-traffic control telecommunications, was the most severe nationwide ground stop since the terrorist attacks of Sept. 11, 2001. It threw airports into chaos, stranded tens of thousands of travelers, and snarled travel through the weekend. Here is how the four-hourlong saga unfolded.
3:12 p.m. ET, Friday
Before the ground stop, communications problems started to crop up, with pilots and controllers reporting static and transmission issues in the airspace near Chicago, Indianapolis, and elsewhere.
3:47 p.m. ET

As communication problems proliferated, controllers appeared to be halting traffic in their respective airports and airspaces. One noted problems at a facility known as a Tracon, or Terminal Radar Approach Control.
3:54 p.m. ET
The FAA issued a nationwide ground stop, halting departures across the country.
4:43 p.m. ET

With flights no longer taking off, airports started to fill up. Some inbound flights had to divert elsewhere in order to find open gates and parking. Messages between airline control rooms and cockpits, known as ACARS messages, describe the challenge.
NO MORE PARKING AT SAN GOING TO NEED ALT ONT OR LAX MAYBE  —  American Airlines Flight 2438
YO YO YO WHATUP BIGDOG ANY UPDATES ON ATC GND STOPS/COMM FAILURE.  —  American Airlines Flight 0358
7 p.m. ET
As the grounding dragged on, airlines began to wind down operations for the night.

GOT WORD FROM MANAGEMENT THE AIRLINE IS SHUTTING DOWN FOR THE NIGHT HAVE EVERYONE OFF THE AIRCRAFT IF YOU HAVE NOT YET DONE SO. EXPECT CANCELLATIONS TO COME THROUGH OVER THE NEXT HOUR  —  ACARS message sent to American Eagle flights operated by Envoy

The ground stop was lifted. But with more than 35% of Friday's flights canceled, planes, pilots and crew members were out of place, and many pilots and flight attendants had hit the limits on how long they can work, leaving airlines with the complex task of reassembling their operations.

NOT SURE IF YOU ARE STILL WITH ME, BUT I HAVE GOOD NEWS. THE GROUND STOP IS PROJECTED TO END SOONISH. PREVIOUSLY THE FAA SAID IT WOULD BE A CONTROLLED AND METERED RELEASE. I EXPECT THIS TO BE A VERY SLUGGISH START TO FLYING. BUT THERE IS HOPE.  —  ACARS message sent to United Airlines Flight 659
